hints: Focus on what each part of the diagram represents, the shape of the curve shows temperature while the marked lines show activation energy.
Remember that heating gives particles more energy, so the peak flattens and shifts right, but the total number of particles stays the same.
Ask yourself whether temperature changes the energy barrier itself, or just how many particles can get over it, for both the catalysed and uncatalysed routes.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the Boltzmann curve shows**

Think of the curve as a spread of energies in the mixture of ethene and hydrogen. The x-axis is energy, $E$, the y-axis is number of particles with that energy. The area under the curve is the total number of particles, so it must stay constant.

**Predict the effect of higher temperature**

At higher $T$, the average energy increases. More particles have high energy and fewer have low energy. So the peak gets lower and moves to the right, and the tail gets longer and flatter. The curve definitely changes shape.

**Check what happens to activation energy**

Activation energy, $E_a$, is the energy barrier for the reaction: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$. A catalyst (nickel) provides a different route with lower $E_a(\text{catalysed})$. Temperature does not change the route, it only changes how many particles have $E \ge E_a$. So both $E_a$ values stay in the same positions on the energy axis.

**Put it together**

Higher temperature flattens and shifts the distribution curve, but leaves the two $E_a$ markers unchanged. That matches the statement that both values remain the same.

options.A: Incorrect. Temperature always changes the distribution of molecular energies. The peak lowers, shifts to higher E, and the curve broadens. Saying it is unchanged ignores the effect of temperature on particle energies.
options.B: Incorrect. This confuses temperature with a catalyst. Only a catalyst (nickel here) lowers $E_a$ by providing an alternative pathway. Raising temperature increases the fraction with $E \ge E_a$, it does not lower $E_a$ itself.
options.C: Incorrect. It is a common trap to think hotter particles need a higher barrier. In fact $E_a$ is fixed for a given reaction pathway at a given set of reactants. Higher temperature just lets more particles overcome the same barrier.
options.D: Correct. The curve shape changes with temperature, but $E_a$ (uncatalysed) and $E_a(\text{catalysed})$ are properties of the reaction routes and do not move. Nickel keeps the catalysed barrier lower, and heating simply increases the area to the right of both markers.
